proposal.title: On the Origin of Species
proposal.gist: Species arise and diverge through natural selection acting on inherited variation in a universal struggle for existence.
proposal.question: Origin of species — why do species resemble yet differ from one another, and how do new ones arise? (a sustained argument)

children.gist: Publication details, title page, epigraphs, and dedication of the first edition.

children.title: Gutenberg edition notice
children.gist: Lists available Gutenberg editions of the book.

children.title: Title and author
children.gist: Full title, subtitle, and author credentials.

children.title: Epigraphs and dedication date
children.gist: Quotations from Whewell and Bacon, and the date and place of writing.

children.title: Detailed table of contents
children.gist: Lists all fourteen chapters with their sub-topics.

children.title: Introduction
children.gist: Darwin explains why he publishes this abstract now and previews the book's argument that species descended with modification mainly through natural selection.
children.question: Origin of species — what is the book's plan and central claim before the evidence is presented? (an overview)

children.title: Origins of the theory
children.gist: Darwin recounts twenty years of fact-gathering since 1837 and the prompting by Wallace's independent paper to publish this abstract now.

children.title: Scope and limits of this abstract
children.gist: The book cannot cite full evidence for each claim, and acknowledges facts on both sides exist for every point discussed.

children.title: Why creation alone fails to explain adaptation
children.gist: Mere descent from other species would not explain how organisms become so finely adapted, as shown by the woodpecker and the mistletoe, so a cause of modification is needed.

children.title: Plan of the volume
children.gist: Darwin previews chapters on domestic variation, natural variation, struggle for existence, selection, and the difficulties and evidence to follow.

children.title: Preliminary statement of the conclusion
children.gist: Species are not immutable but are modified descendants of earlier species, with natural selection as the main, though not sole, means of modification.

children.title: Variation Under Domestication
children.gist: Breeders unconsciously and methodically accumulate small inherited variations in domestic plants and animals, producing breeds as different as if they were separate species.
children.question: Variation under domestication — how does human selection reshape living things, and what does that reveal about change in nature? (several lines of evidence)

children.title: Causes and character of variability
children.gist: Changed conditions of life, acting mainly on the reproductive system, make domesticated organisms far more variable than their wild relatives, with variability continuing across many generations.

children.title: Inheritance and reversion
children.gist: Most variations, however slight or rare, are inherited, and domestic varieties sometimes revert toward ancestral characters rather than losing acquired traits entirely.

children.title: Pigeon breeds as a case study
children.gist: Despite extreme differences among fancy pigeon breeds in beak, skeleton, and plumage, converging evidence of behavior, fertility, and reversion colors shows they all descend from the wild rock-pigeon.

children.title: Methodical and unconscious selection
children.gist: Breeders both deliberately and unintentionally accumulate tiny favorable differences over generations, a slow cumulative process that has produced strikingly distinct breeds without any single large change.

children.title: Conditions favoring selection
children.gist: Large numbers of individuals, careful attention to the valued trait, and prevention of unwanted crossing are what allow human selection to produce new breeds, just as similar conditions will matter for selection in nature.

children.title: Variation Under Nature
children.gist: In wild species, individual variation blurs the line between variety and species, and this variability is greatest precisely in the common, widespread species of large genera.
children.question: Variation under nature — do wild species vary as domestic ones do, and what pattern does that variation follow? (a statistical survey)

children.title: Species, varieties, and individual differences
children.gist: No sharp line separates individual differences, varieties, and species, since naturalists disagree endlessly about which doubtful forms deserve which rank, suggesting the categories blend into one another.

children.title: Doubtful forms as incipient species
children.gist: Forms that naturalists cannot confidently rank as species or varieties are best understood as varieties in the process of becoming distinct species through accumulated natural selection.

children.title: Variability tied to dominance
children.gist: Darwin's tabulations of floras show that the most common, widely diffused, dominant species of larger genera are exactly those that produce the most varieties, as if a manufactory of new forms stays active where it has already been productive.

children.title: Large genera resemble clusters of varieties
children.gist: Species in large genera are packed more closely together, with smaller average differences and more restricted ranges, so that they themselves resemble varieties clustered around dominant parent forms.

children.title: Struggle for Existence
children.gist: Because every organism tends to multiply far beyond what resources allow, a constant struggle for life ensues that favors any individual with even a slight advantage over its competitors.
children.question: Struggle for existence — why must such a struggle occur, and what shapes who wins it? (an argument from population growth)

children.title: Meaning and inevitability of the struggle
children.gist: Darwin defines struggle broadly to include dependence between organisms and reproductive success, and shows it follows necessarily from every species' tendency to increase geometrically beyond available resources.

children.title: Checks on increase: climate, food, and enemies
children.gist: Numbers are held in check by shifting combinations of climate, food supply, and predators or competitors, illustrated by cases from English heaths to Scotch fir plantations where a single change cascades through many species.

children.title: Webs of dependency among species
children.gist: Darwin traces how cats affect mice, mice affect bees, and bees affect clover, showing that the number of any species depends on an intricate, often hidden web of relations to other organisms, not on physical conditions alone.

children.title: Competition fiercest among close relations
children.gist: Because they share needs and habits, the struggle for existence is generally most severe between individuals of the same species and between closely related species, which is why advantageous variations there matter most.

children.title: Natural Selection
children.gist: Natural selection preserves favorable variations and destroys harmful ones far more effectively than human breeders, gradually adapting organisms and causing their characters to diverge and multiply into new species.
children.question: Natural selection — how does unguided nature achieve what breeders achieve on purpose, and what follows from it? (the book's central mechanism)

children.title: Definition of natural selection
children.gist: Given variation, heredity, and a struggle in which more are born than can survive, individuals with any advantage will tend to survive and reproduce, and Darwin names this preservation of favorable variation natural selection.

children.title: Nature's selection surpasses man's
children.gist: Because nature can act on every part of an organism over vast spans of time, judged solely by fitness rather than human convenience, its power of selection vastly exceeds anything breeders achieve.

children.title: Sexual selection
children.gist: Competition among males for mates, through combat or female preference, explains traits like antlers and plumage that serve courtship rather than survival, operating by a weaker form of selection than ordinary natural selection.

children.title: Illustrations: wolves and flowers
children.gist: Hypothetical cases of wolves varying in speed and of flowers evolving nectar and separated sexes to attract pollinators show concretely how small advantageous variations could be preserved and compounded over time.

children.title: Why intercrossing matters
children.gist: Darwin argues from widespread evidence that even hermaphrodite plants and animals benefit from occasional crossing with another individual, a law of nature that explains many otherwise puzzling floral structures.

children.title: Conditions governing selection's power
children.gist: Variability, large populations, and partial isolation favor natural selection, and comparing isolated islands with large continents suggests that extensive, variously conditioned areas produce the most successful and widely spreading new species.

children.title: Extinction as selection's counterpart
children.gist: As favored forms increase, less-favored ones inevitably become rare and die out, so that extinction of old species and production of new ones are two sides of the same selective process.

children.title: Divergence of character
children.gist: Because the greatest number of beings can be supported where structure and habits are most diversified, natural selection favors increasing divergence among a species' descendants, explaining how small variety-level differences grow into the larger gaps that separate genera.

children.title: Chapter summary and the tree of life
children.gist: Variation, struggle, inheritance, and divergence together explain why organisms fall into groups within groups, naturally pictured as a great branching tree where most early twigs have died and only a few branches survive to flourish today.

children.title: Laws of Variation
children.gist: Variation follows complex laws—use and disuse, correlated growth, and conditions of life—that interact with natural selection to shape structure, rather than variation being purely random.
children.question: Laws of variation — what patterns govern how organisms vary, beyond natural selection itself? (a survey of contributing causes)

children.title: Effects of conditions, use and disuse
children.gist: Changed conditions of life induce variability mainly by disturbing reproduction, while long-continued use or disuse of organs, as in flightless beetles and blind cave animals, can enlarge or reduce structures independent of or alongside selection.

children.title: Acclimatisation and habit
children.gist: Species show real but limited ability to become habituated to new climates through a mix of inherited habit and the selection of individuals with suitable constitutions, as shown by transplanted pines and variably hardy seedlings.

children.title: Correlation and compensation of growth
children.gist: Because the whole organism is tied together during development, a change in one part—such as color, horn shape, or seed structure—often drags other parts along with it, independent of any direct usefulness.

children.title: Variability of repeated, rudimentary, and specific parts
children.gist: Parts that are repeated many times, left over as rudiments, or distinguish species rather than genera tend to be the most variable, because natural selection has least rigidly fixed their exact form.

children.title: Analogous variation and reversion
children.gist: Related species and domestic breeds often vary in parallel ways or revert to ancestral traits, such as the recurring blue-and-barred pattern in pigeons or stripes in horse-family animals, because they share an inherited tendency to vary similarly.

children.title: Chapter summary
children.gist: Though the deep causes of variation remain largely unknown, the same patterns of correlated, repeated, and reversionary change recur whether comparing individuals, varieties, or species, supporting their common origin.

children.title: Difficulties on Theory
children.gist: Darwin confronts the gravest objections to his theory—missing transitional forms, complex organs, instinct, and sterility—and argues each is explicable rather than fatal.
children.question: Difficulties on theory — do the hardest objections actually refute natural selection? (four objections answered)

children.title: Why transitional varieties are rare
children.gist: Natural selection's own logic—that improved forms exterminate their less-fit parents and competitors—explains why intermediate forms are scarce today and preserved only patchily in the fossil record.

children.title: Transitions between habits and structures
children.gist: Living examples of animals with intermediate habits, like swimming carnivores, gliding squirrels, and tree-climbing woodpeckers that never climb trees, show that drastic differences in way of life can be bridged by functional intermediate stages.

children.title: The evolution of complex organs like the eye
children.gist: Though an organ as perfect as the eye seems impossible to produce gradually, a graded series from a simple light-sensitive nerve to a complex eye exists among living animals, showing such perfection could accumulate by numerous small useful steps.

children.title: Organs of trifling importance and imperfect adaptation
children.gist: Many small or seemingly useless features, like a giraffe's fly-flapping tail, can still matter enough for survival to be shaped by selection, and nature's imperfect designs, like the self-destroying bee sting, confirm selection works through accumulated net advantage rather than engineered perfection.

children.title: Natura non facit saltum and unity of type
children.gist: The old naturalists' rule that nature makes no leaps, along with the twin laws of unity of type and adaptation to conditions, both follow naturally from descent with modification through gradual natural selection.

children.title: Instinct
children.gist: Complex instincts, including slave-making ants and the bee's cell-building, can arise through the same gradual accumulation of small variations as bodily structure, without requiring reason or conscious design.
children.question: Instinct — can behavior as intricate as a bee building a honeycomb evolve the way organs do? (three case studies)

children.title: Instinct compared to habit
children.gist: Instinct resembles habit in its unconscious, rhythmic performance, and inherited habitual actions can become indistinguishable from true instincts, though most complex instincts are not simply learned habits passed down.

children.title: Domestic instincts as evidence of change
children.gist: Breeds of dogs and pigeons show inherited behavioral tendencies, such as pointing or tumbling, that arose from selected natural variations rather than training, demonstrating that instincts do vary and can be shaped by selection.

children.title: The cuckoo and parasitic instincts
children.gist: The cuckoo's habit of laying eggs in other birds' nests likely began as an occasional habit among egg-laying birds that was advantageous and so became fixed, a pattern paralleled by parasitic bees and wasps.

children.title: Slave-making ants
children.gist: Darwin's own observations of Formica sanguinea alongside the fully dependent Formica rufescens show graded degrees of reliance on captured workers, suggesting the extreme instinct evolved from an ordinary habit of collecting pupae as food.

children.title: The hive-bee's cell-building instinct
children.gist: Through comparison with humble-bees and the intermediate Melipona, and confirmed by experiments on wax combs, Darwin shows the bee's seemingly perfect hexagonal cells result from simple instincts of equal spacing and wax economy, not geometric genius.

children.title: Sterile worker insects as a special difficulty
children.gist: Though sterile workers cannot pass on their own traits, selection acting on the fertile parents that produce them can still shape worker structure and instinct across generations, resolving what first seemed a fatal problem for the theory.

children.title: Hybridism
children.gist: The sterility separating species from each other is not a special created barrier but an incidental and variable byproduct of differences in their reproductive systems, paralleling the fertility effects of crossing and disturbed conditions.
children.question: Hybridism — why are species usually sterile together while varieties are not, and what does that difference really mean? (a comparative survey)

children.title: Degrees and inconsistency of hybrid sterility
children.gist: Careful study of plant crosses shows that sterility between species varies continuously from none to total and is easily disturbed by cultivation conditions, undermining any sharp rule distinguishing species from varieties by fertility alone.

children.title: Laws governing sterility
children.gist: Sterility in first crosses and hybrids does not track systematic closeness in any simple way, differs between reciprocal crosses of the same two species, and parallels the way grafting succeeds or fails between related plants for unknown reasons.

children.title: Causes: disturbed reproductive systems
children.gist: Hybrid sterility resembles the sterility caused in pure species by unnatural conditions of life, since in both cases an organism's reproductive system has been disturbed, here by having two distinct constitutions blended into one.

children.title: Fertility of crossed varieties and its limits
children.gist: Varieties usually cross fully fertilely, but some well-documented exceptions among maize, gourds, and verbascum show this fertility is not an absolute rule either, further blurring any strict species-variety boundary based on sterility.

children.title: Hybrids and mongrels compared
children.gist: Aside from their differing fertility, crossed offspring of species and crossed offspring of varieties behave very similarly in variability and resemblance to parents, consistent with there being no essential distinction between species and varieties.

children.title: Imperfection of the Geological Record
children.gist: The fossil record is far too incomplete, with vast unrecorded time and patchy preservation, to show the countless transitional forms the theory requires, resolving what otherwise seems a fatal gap in the evidence.
children.question: Geological record — why don't we find the innumerable transitional fossils the theory predicts? (an argument from incompleteness)

children.title: What transitional forms would actually look like
children.gist: Transitional links connect each species to a shared ancestor, not directly to each other, so we should not expect to find forms directly between living species like the horse and tapir, only between each and an unknown common parent.

children.title: The vast and barely imaginable lapse of time
children.gist: Evidence from coastal erosion, sediment thickness, and denudation of the Weald shows that geological time vastly exceeds ordinary intuition, providing ample time for gradual change even though it strains the imagination.

children.title: Why fossil collections are so poor
children.gist: Soft-bodied creatures, shallow seas, and rare favorable burial conditions mean only a tiny, biased fraction of past life has ever been preserved as fossils, especially from before the tertiary period.

children.title: Intermittent formations and blank intervals
children.gist: Thick fossil-bearing strata accumulate only during subsidence with matched sedimentation, so formations are separated by enormous blank intervals during which erosion, not deposition, dominates, erasing most of the record.

children.title: Sudden appearances explained by migration and gaps
children.gist: Species and whole groups that seem to appear abruptly in strata likely existed and diversified elsewhere first, immigrating into the examined region only after enormous unrecorded intervals of time had already passed.

children.title: The unexplained gap before the Silurian strata
children.gist: The absence of fossils beneath the earliest known Silurian rocks remains a genuinely unresolved puzzle, though Darwin speculates that oceans and continents may have occupied roughly their present positions since before any known fossil record.

children.title: Geological Succession of Organic Beings
children.gist: The order, rate, and affinities of fossils across geological time match what gradual, branching descent with natural selection predicts far better than a picture of fixed, independently created species.
children.question: Geological succession — does the sequence of fossils through time support gradual transformation of species? (a pattern-by-pattern comparison)

children.title: Gradual and unequal rates of change
children.gist: New species appear slowly and one by one rather than all at once, and different lineages change at very different rates, exactly as expected if each species' modification depends on its own particular competitive circumstances.

children.title: Extinction as ordinary and continuous
children.gist: Rather than being swept away by catastrophes, species and groups disappear gradually, rarity typically preceding extinction just as sickness precedes death, and a species once lost never reappears in the same form.

children.title: Worldwide parallel succession of forms
children.gist: Marine faunas across the globe change in parallel at roughly the same broad periods, which Darwin explains by the spread and gradual replacement of dominant, widely varying species rather than by any special law tied to climate.

children.title: Affinities of extinct to living forms
children.gist: Ancient fossils tend to fall intermediate in character between groups that have since diverged further apart, and each geological period's fauna is roughly intermediate between the faunas before and after it, just as common descent predicts.

children.title: Succession of types within the same regions
children.gist: Fossil mammals in Australia and South America closely resemble the living mammals of those same continents, a geographic continuity of type best explained by true descent of modern inhabitants from these extinct relatives.

children.title: Chapter summary
children.gist: All the major patterns of fossil succession—gradual change, extinction, parallel worldwide timing, intermediate affinities, and regional continuity of type—converge to support descent with modification over independent creation.

children.title: Geographical Distribution
children.gist: Where species live is explained far better by migration from a single birthplace, shaped by barriers and past climate change, than by independent creation suited to local conditions.
children.question: Geographical distribution — why do similar places have different inhabitants, and distant similar species share no climate? (barriers versus conditions)

children.title: Climate fails, barriers succeed as explanations
children.gist: Regions with nearly identical climates, like parts of Australia, Africa, and South America, have utterly different inhabitants, while barriers like oceans and deserts closely track where distinct faunas begin and end.

children.title: Single birthplace and subsequent migration
children.gist: Despite real difficulties explaining how any one species reached its scattered locations, Darwin argues each species arose in one region and spread from there, since this simple view accounts far better for the overwhelming importance of barriers than does multiple independent creation.

children.title: Means of dispersal across barriers
children.gist: Experiments and observations on floating, salt-resistant seeds, seeds carried in mud, birds' feet and crops, and drifting icebergs show numerous real, if occasional, ways that plants and small animals could cross seas and found new populations far from their origin.

children.title: The Glacial period and shared mountain floras
children.gist: A worldwide glacial episode drove cold-adapted species southward together and then let them retreat, stranding identical or closely allied species on separated mountain-tops and in both polar regions, explaining their otherwise puzzling shared distribution.

children.title: Geographical Distribution, continued
children.gist: The special patterns of freshwater life and of oceanic island inhabitants likewise point to migration, colonization, and subsequent modification rather than separate creation suited to each place.
children.question: Island and freshwater life — why are these inhabitants so distinctive yet so clearly linked to a nearby mainland? (further case studies)

children.title: Wide dispersal of freshwater species
children.gist: Despite seeming isolated by land barriers, freshwater fish, shells, and plants range surprisingly widely because ducks, herons, and other mobile creatures transport their eggs, seeds, and young between separate ponds and rivers.

children.title: Oceanic islands: scarcity and peculiarity
children.gist: Oceanic islands have few species overall but a strikingly high proportion found nowhere else, a pattern of scarcity plus endemism that fits occasional difficult colonization followed by isolated modification, not creation tailored to each island.

children.title: Missing groups: frogs, mammals, and bats
children.gist: The near-total absence of frogs and land mammals from remote oceanic islands, despite suitable conditions, alongside the regular presence of bats which can fly there, is explained by transport difficulty rather than any special creative design.

children.title: Islands related to their nearest mainland
children.gist: Galapagos and Cape Verde species, though peculiar to their own islands, unmistakably resemble those of the nearest continent rather than islands with similar climate elsewhere, showing colonization from the nearest source followed by modification.

children.title: Summary of distribution chapters
children.gist: Allowing for our ignorance of past climate change and transport methods, nearly every major pattern of distribution—barriers, endemism, island poverty, and mainland affinity—is explicable by migration and modification from single origins.

children.title: Classification, Morphology, Embryology, Rudimentary Organs
children.gist: Shared body plans, embryonic resemblance, and useless vestigial organs all make sense as traces of common ancestry, revealing that natural classification is really a genealogical record of descent.
children.question: Classification and structure — what do shared patterns and useless organs reveal about relatedness? (four converging kinds of evidence)

children.title: Classification reflects genealogy, not mere similarity
children.gist: Naturalists already rank organisms by subordinate groups, favor physiologically unimportant but constant characters, and value rudimentary organs and embryonic resemblance, all practices that make sense if classification is secretly tracking common descent.

children.title: True affinity versus adaptive resemblance
children.gist: Superficial similarities from shared habits, like the fish-like shape of whales and dugongs, are distinguished by naturalists from true affinities of common descent, because adaptive resemblance can mislead about real relatedness while inherited structure reveals it.

children.title: Morphology: shared patterns across species and organs
children.gist: The same bones recur in a human hand, bat wing, and horse leg, and the same elemental parts recur across an individual's own skull, limbs, or flower parts, because all were inherited with modification from a common, simpler ancestral pattern.

children.title: Embryology: why embryos resemble each other more than adults
children.gist: Because successive variations in a lineage tend to appear and be inherited at the same later stage of life, embryos of very different adult animals preserve a shared, less modified ancestral form, making embryonic resemblance a clue to common descent.

children.title: Rudimentary organs as traces of ancestry
children.gist: Useless structures like vestigial teeth in whale embryos or shriveled insect wings result from disuse reducing organs mainly in adults while inheritance preserves them relatively unaltered in the embryo, marking the former functional state of an ancestor.

children.title: Recapitulation and Conclusion
children.gist: Weighing the real difficulties against the much larger body of converging evidence, Darwin concludes that all organic beings have descended with modification from a few, or even one, primordial forms.
children.question: Recapitulation — on balance, does the evidence for descent with modification outweigh its remaining difficulties? (final judgment)

children.title: Difficulties reconsidered
children.gist: Darwin reviews the objections from complex organs, hybrid sterility, imperfect distribution evidence, and the missing geological links, arguing each is explicable given our admitted ignorance rather than fatal to the theory.

children.title: The positive case restated
children.gist: Variability under domestication, the struggle for existence, and natural selection's power to accumulate favorable variations together explain classification, morphology, embryology, rudimentary organs, and the geological and geographic patterns surveyed throughout the book.

children.title: Why naturalists resist the mutability of species
children.gist: Deep-seated habits of mind, not any decisive evidence, explain the near-universal belief in fixed species, since immutability seemed natural when geological time was thought short and transitional steps remain unseen.

children.title: Extending the theory and its future implications
children.gist: Darwin extends descent with modification to all members of each class and perhaps to one primordial form, and predicts a coming revolution in natural history, geology, and even the future study of human psychology.

children.title: Concluding reflection
children.gist: Darwin closes by finding grandeur rather than diminishment in the view that nature's simple fixed laws of growth, inheritance, variation, and selection have produced endless beautiful and wonderful forms from a simple beginning.

children.title: Index
children.gist: An alphabetical index of names, topics, and terms covered in the book.
